# [Thursday 24 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/24/)

A cold day. Up, and to [the Office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the morning alone at the Office, nobody meeting, being the eve of [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/). At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then to the Office busy, all the afternoon, and at night home to supper, and it being now very cold, and in hopes of a frost, I begin this night to put on a [waistcoat](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10449/), it being the first winter in my whole memory that ever I staid till this day before I did so. So to bed in mighty good humour with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), but sad, in one thing, and that is for my poor eyes.

[Read 6 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/24/#annotations)

# [Friday 25 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/25/)

([Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/)-day). Up, and continued on my [waistcoat](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10449/), the first day this winter, and I to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), where [Alderman Backewell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/967/), coming in late, I beckoned to [his lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4900/) to come up to us, who did, with another lady; and after sermon, I led her down through the church to her husband and coach, a noble, fine woman, and a good one, and one my wife shall be acquainted with. So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and to dinner alone with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), who, poor wretch! sat undressed all day, till ten at night, altering and lacing of a noble petticoat: while I by her, making [the boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/) read to me the [Life of Julius Caesar](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13129/), and [Des Cartes’](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6622/)[book of Musick](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12334/) — the latter of which I understand not, nor think he did well that writ it, though a most learned man. Then, after supper, I made the boy play upon his [lute](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/540/), which I have not done twice before since he come to me; and so, my mind in mighty content, we to bed.

[Read 10 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/25/#annotations)

# [Saturday 26 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/26/)

Lay long with pleasure, prating with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and then up, and I a little to [the Office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and my head busy setting some papers and accounts to rights, which being long neglected because of my eyes will take me up much time and care to do, but it must be done. So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) at noon to dinner, and then abroad with my wife to a play, at the [Duke of York’s house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2935/), the house full of ordinary citizens. The play was [“Women Pleased,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13130/) which we had never seen before; and, though but indifferent, yet there is a good design for a good play. So home, and there to talk, and my wife to read to me, and so to bed.

[Read 6 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/26/#annotations)

# [Sunday 27 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/27/)

(Lord’s day). Walked to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) and there saw [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) at [chapel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1042/); but staid not to hear anything, but went to walk in [the Park](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/), with [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/), who was with me; and there, among others, met with [Sir G. Downing](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/106/), and walked with him an hour, talking of business, and how the [late war](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13153/) was managed, there being nobody to take care of it, and telling how, when he was in Holland, what he offered the King to do, if he might have power, and they would give him power, and then, upon the least word, perhaps of a woman, to the King, he was contradicted again, and particularly to the loss of all that we lost in [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/). He told me that he had so good spies, that he hath had the keys taken out of [De Witt’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8718/) pocket when he was a-bed, and his closet opened, and papers brought to him, and left in his hands for an hour, and carried back and laid in the place again, and keys put into his pocket again. He says that he hath always had their most private debates, that have been but between two or three of the chief of them, brought to him in an hour after, and an hour after that, hath sent word thereof to the King, but nobody here regarded them. But he tells me the sad news, that he is out of all expectations that ever the debts of the Navy will be paid, if the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) do not enable the King to do it by money; all they can hope for to do out of the King’s revenue being but to keep our wheels a-going on present services, and, if they can, to cut off the growing interest: which is a sad story, and grieves me to the heart.

So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), my coach coming for me, and there find [Balty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/) and [Mr. How](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/549/), who dined with me; and there [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I fell out a little about the foulness of the linen of the table, but were friends presently, but she cried, poor heart! which I was troubled for, though I did not give her one hard word.

Dinner done, she to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and W. How and I all the afternoon talking together about my [Lord Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) suffering his business of the [prizes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/) to be managed by [Sir R. Cuttance](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/583/), who is so deep in the business, more than my Lord knows of, and such a loggerhead, and under such prejudice, that he will, we doubt, do my Lord much wrong. In the evening, he gone, my wife to read to me and talk, and spent the evening with much pleasure, and so to supper and to bed.

# [Monday 28 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/28/)

Up, called up by drums and [trumpets](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10492/); these things and boxes [??] having cost me much money this [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/) already, and will do more. [My wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) down by water to see [her mother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1066/), and I with [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) all day together in my closet making some advance in the settling of my accounts, which have been so long unevened that it troubles me how to set them right, having not the use of my eyes to help me. My wife at night [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and tells me how much her mother prays for me and is troubled for my eyes; and I am glad to have friendship with them, and believe they are truly glad to see their daughter come to live so well as she do. So spent the night in talking, and so to supper and to bed.

[Read 29 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/28/#annotations)

# [Tuesday 29 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/29/)

Up, and at [the Office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, and at noon to dinner, and there, by a pleasant mistake, find my [uncle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/911/) and [aunt Wight](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/995/), and three more of their company, come to dine with me to-day, thinking that they had been invited, which they were not; but yet we did give them a pretty good dinner, and mighty merry at the mistake. They sat most of the afternoon with us, and then parted, and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I out, thinking to have gone to a play, but it was too far begun, and so to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and there she and I bought several things, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), with much pleasure talking, and then to reading, and so to supper and to bed.

[Read 7 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/29/#annotations)

# [Wednesday 30 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/30/)

Up, and vexed a little to be forced to pay 40 _s._ for a glass of my coach, which was broke the other day, nobody knows how, within the door, while it was down; but I do doubt that I did break it myself with my knees. After dinner, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I to the [Duke’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2935/), and there did see [King Harry the Eighth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7044/); and was mightily pleased, better than I ever expected, with the history and shows of it. We happened to sit by [Mr. Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7673/), our neighbour, and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8645/), who talked so fondly to his little boy. Thence my wife and I to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/); but, in going, our neere horse did fling himself, kicking of the coachbox over the pole; and a great deal of trouble it was to get him right again, and we forced to ’light, and in great fear of spoiling the horse, but there was no hurt. So to the ’Change, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there spent the evening talking, and so to supper and to bed.

[Read 21 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/30/#annotations)

# [Thursday 31 December 1668](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1668/12/31/)

Up, and at the Office all the morning. At noon [Capt. Ferrers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/727/) and [Mr. Sheres](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11574/) come to me to dinner, who did, and pretty pleased with their talk of Spayne; but [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) did not come down, I suppose because she would not, Captain Ferrers being there, to oblige me by it. They gone, after dinner, I to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and then in the evening [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), being the last day of the year, to endeavour to pay all bills and servants’ wages, &c., which I did almost to 5 _l._ that I know that I owe in the world, but to the publique; and so with great pleasure to supper and to bed, and, blessed be God! the year ends, after some late very great sorrow with my wife by my folly, yet ends, I say, with great mutual peace and content, and likely to last so by my care, who am resolved to enjoy the sweet of it, which I now possess, by never giving her like cause of trouble. My greatest trouble is now from the backwardness of my accounts, which I have not seen the bottom of now near these two years, so that I know not in what condition I am in the world, but by the grace of God, as far as my eyes will give me leave, I will do it.

# Wednesday 5 December 1660

This morning the Proposal which I wrote the last night I showed to [the officers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1121/) this morning, and was well liked of, and I wrote it fair for [Sir. G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) to show to [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), and so it is to go to the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/).

I dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and after dinner I went to [the new Theatre](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1611/) and there I saw [“The Merry Wives of Windsor”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5443/) acted, the humours of the country gentleman and the French doctor very well done, but the rest but very poorly, and Sir J. Falstaffe as bad as any.

From thence to [Mr. Will. Montagu’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/563/) chamber to have sealed some writings tonight between [Sir R. Parkhurst](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1660/) and myself about [my Lord’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) 2000 _l._, but he not coming, I went to [my father’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) and there found [my mother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/282/) still ill of [the stone](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/346/), and had just newly voided one, which she had let drop into the chimney, and looked and found it to shew it me.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/05/#fn1-1660-12-05) From thence home and to bed.

1.   Instead of “which she had let drop into the chimney, and looked and found it to shew it me,” Latham & Matthews have it, “which she hath let drop into the Chimny; and _could not_ find it to show it me.” (emphasis mine) P.G. [↩](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/12/05/#fnr1-1660-12-05)

This is very complicated. "... the humble household of his father, a taylor, ..."

I agree the senior Pepys were not wealthy, but sometimes I think we take the humble and poor story a tad too far.

John Pepys lives in a house in Salisbury Court (where some wealthy people also lived) which was big enough for a family of 5. 

They sent 2 sons to University, on scholarships yes, but nevertheless that was years of schooling when the boys could have been earning and contributing money to the famly. 

Just a few months ago at least one of Sandwich's servants was living with them -- not enough room for everyone at Whitehall apparently.

In a couple of years about three of Sandwich's daughters (presumably with maids) are sent to stay with John for the summer at Brampton -- sorry, a very minor spoiler -- when smallpox breaks out at Hinchingbrooke. 

So although we do not hear of mum and dad Pepys going to lunch with M'Lord, they were clearly part of the extended Sandwich network in good standing.

John Sr. belongs to the Merchant Tailors Company, which cost money. Annotators have presumed Pepys doesn't always have his clothes made by his father was because John was a mediocre tailor -- maybe he was so good he was too busy to accommodate his son's quick-turn-around demands?

Were they wealthy? No. But John Sr. hasn't asked Sam for any money either, beyond being paid for the work he performed. He sounds like a proud father to me.

And Mrs. Pepys Sr. sounds like she has done some scrimping and saving to educate her boys -- e.g. used daughter Pall instead of hiring a live-in maid -- and was somewhat disappointed in her life, so she turned to Puritanism for answers. She also had rich relatives, and consequently unmet aspirations.

They could afford the coal to make those smoldering ashes. Many could not.

# Monday 30 December 1667

Up before day, and by coach to Westminster, and there first to [Sir H. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/), and there I did to my great content deliver him up his little several papers for sums of money paid him, and took his regular receipts upon his orders, wherein I am safe. Thence to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there to visit [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/), and there was with him a great while, and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4039/) and they seem in very good humour, but by and by Sir G. Carteret and I alone, and there we did talk of the ruinous condition we are in, [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) being going to put out of the Council so many able men; such as my [Lord Anglesey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/887/), [Ashly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/215/), [Hollis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/886/), [Secretary Morrice](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5947/) (to bring in [Mr. Trevor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11972/)), and the [Archbishop of Canterbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/), and my [Lord Bridgewater](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11086/). He tells me that this is true, only the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) do endeavour to hinder it, and the Duke of York himself did tell him so: that the King and the Duke of York do not in company disagree, but are friendly; but that there is a core in their hearts, he doubts, which is not to be easily removed; for these men do suffer only for their constancy to the [Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/), or at least from the King’s ill-will against him: that they do now all they can to vilify the clergy, and do accuse [Rochester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10263/) [Dolben] … [of his being given to boys and of his putting his hand into a gentleman (who now comes to bear evidence against him) his codpiece while they were at table together. – L&M] And so do raise scandals, all that is possible, against other of the Bishops. He do suggest that something is intended for the [Duke of Monmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5315/), and it may be, against [the Queene](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) also: that we are in no manner sure against an invasion the next year: that the [Duke of Buckingham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2558/) do rule all now, and the Duke of York comes indeed to [the Caball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), but signifies little there. That this new faction do not endure, nor the King, [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/); but yet that he is so usefull that they cannot be without him; but that he is not now called to the Caball. That my Lord of Buckingham, [Bristoll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2845/), and [Arlington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5520/), do seem to agree in these things; but that they do not in their hearts trust one another, but do drive several ways, all of them. In short, he do bless himself that he is no more concerned in matters now; and the hopes he hath of being at liberty, when his accounts are over, to retire into the country. That he do give over the kingdom for wholly lost. So after some other little discourse, I away, meeting with [Mr. Cooling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1027/). I with him by coach to [the Wardrobe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/946/), where I never was since [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/) in [Hatton Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10948/), but did not ’light: and he tells me he fears that my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) will suffer much by [Mr. Townsend’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/947/) being untrue to him, he being now unable to give the [Commissioners of the Treasury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11226/) an account of his money received by many thousands of pounds, which I am troubled for.

Thence to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) together, he telling me that he believes there will be no such turning out of great men as is talked of, but that it is only to fright people, but I do fear there may be such a thing doing. He do mightily inveigh against the folly of the King to bring his matters to wrack thus, and that we must all be undone without help. I met with Cooling at the [Temple-gate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/503/), after I had been at both [my](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11024/)[booksellers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11465/) and there laid out several pounds in books now against the new year. From the ’Change (where I met with [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), who would have borrowed money of me, but I had the grace to deny him, he would have had 3 or 400 _l._) I with Cocke and [Mr. Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9022/) (whose wife was just now brought to bed of a boy, but he seems not to be at all taken with it, which is a strange consideration how others do rejoice to have a child born), to Sir G. Carteret’s, in [Lincoln’s Inn Fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/125/), and there did dine together, there being there, among other company, [Mr. Attorney Montagu](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/563/), and [his fine lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3690/), a fine woman. After dinner, I did understand from my [Lady Jemimah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/114/) that her brother [Hinchingbroke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/113/) business was to be ended this day, as she thinks, towards his match, and they do talk here of their intent to buy themselves some new clothes against the wedding, which I am very glad of. After dinner I did even with Sir G. Carteret the accounts of the interest of the money which I did so long put out for him in [Sir R. Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) hands, and by it I think I shall be a gainer about 28 _l._, which is a very good reward for the little trouble I have had in it. Thence with [Sir Philip Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8250/) to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), there to see [“Love’s Cruelty,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11973/) an old play, but which I have not seen before; and in the first act [Orange Moll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10310/) come to me, with one of our porters by my house, to tell me that [Mrs. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/) and [Knepp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9483/) did dine at my house to-day, and that I was desired to come [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). So I went out presently, and by coach home, and they were just gone away so, after a very little stay with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), I took coach again, and to the King’s playhouse again, and come in the fourth act; and it proves to me a very silly play, and to everybody else, as far as I could judge. But the jest is, that here telling Moll how I had lost my journey, she told me that Mrs. Knepp was in the house, and so shews me to her, and I went to her, and sat out the play, and then with her to [Mrs. Manuel’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11497/), where Mrs. Pierce was, and her [boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9472/) and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9044/); and here I did hear Mrs. Manuel and one of the Italians, her gallant, sing well. But yet I confess I am not delighted so much with it, as to admire it: for, not understanding the words, I lose the benefit of the vocalitys of the musick, and it proves only instrumental; and therefore was more pleased to hear Knepp sing two or three little English things that I understood, though the composition of the other, and performance, was very fine. Thence, after sitting and talking a pretty while, I took leave and left them there, and so to my bookseller’s, and paid for the books I had bought, and away home, where I told my wife where I had been. But she was as mad as a devil, and nothing but ill words between us all the evening while we sat at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) — [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) and [the girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) by — even to gross ill words, which I was troubled for, but do see that I must use policy to keep her spirit down, and to give her no offence by my being with Knepp and Pierce, of which, though she will not own it, yet she is heartily jealous. At last it ended in few words and my silence (which for fear of growing higher between us I did forbear), and so to supper and to bed without one word one to another.

This day I did carry money out, and paid several debts. Among others, [my tailor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9587/), and shoemaker, and draper, [Sir W. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3725/), who begun to talk of the [Commission of accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/), wherein he is one; but though they are the greatest people that ever were in the nation as to power, and like to be our judges, yet I did never speak one word to him of desiring favour, or bidding him joy in it, but did answer him to what he said, and do resolve to stand or fall by my silent preparing to answer whatever can be laid to me, and that will be my best proceeding, I think. This day I got a little rent in my new fine [camlett](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11928/) cloak with the latch of Sir G. Carteret’s door; but it is darned up at my tailor’s, that it will be no great blemish to it; but it troubled me. I could not but observe that Sir Philip Carteret would fain have given me my going into a play; but yet, when he come to the door, he had no money to pay for himself, I having refused to accept of it for myself, but was fain; and I perceive he is known there, and do run upon the score for plays, which is a shame; but I perceive always he is in want of money.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/30/#fn1-1667-12-30)

In the pit I met with [Sir Ch. North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/725/), formerly Mr. North, who was with my Lord at sea; and he, of his own accord, was so silly as to tell me he [is married](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11974/); and for her quality (being a Lord’s daughter, my Lord Grey), and person, and beauty, and years, and estate, and disposition, he is the happiest man in the world. I am sure he is an ugly fellow; but a good scholar and sober gentleman; and heir to his father, now [Lord North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/726/), the [old Lord](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14142/) being dead.

Phew! Quite a entry.

"and in the first act Orange Moll come to me, with one of our porters by my house, to tell me that Mrs. Pierce and Knepp did dine at my house to-day, and that I was desired to come home. So I went out presently, and by coach home, and they were just gone away so, after a very little stay with my wife,"

Oh, the possibilities for the imagination...How did Bess know where Sam was unless Pierce or Knipp suggested it? And how joyful she must have been at that hint, if made. And the dinner itself...Had Sam thoughlessly organized the most repulsive company possible for poor suffering Bess and then forgotton his own party? Or had Bess bitten the bullet and braved the supposed, but alas wrong, enemy...The real if involuntionary one helpfully standing at her side...In her own den? And the very little stay...

Followed by...

"and away home, where I told my wife where I had been. But she was as mad as a devil, and nothing but ill words between us all the evening while we sat at cards — W. Hewer and the girl by — even to gross ill words, which I was troubled for, but do see that I must use policy to keep her spirit down, and to give her no offence by my being with Knepp and Pierce, of which, though she will not own it, yet she is heartily jealous. At last it ended in few words and my silence (which for fear of growing higher between us I did forbear), and so to supper and to bed without one word one to another."

Speaking such volumes one hopes Sam had tongue firmly in cheek writing some of this. But hey, what possibly could have irritated the woman so?

It's as if Sam takes what in other men would simply be gross insensitivity and crafts it into a whole glorious new art form, spiraling off in directions one could never imagine until, greatest irony of all, he winds up paying perhaps one of the sweetest tributes to a suffering wife any man ever has. Cause after all, he could have torn this out and cast it into the fire at any time. And Elisabeth lives forever...Reminding us what a dunderheaded jerk her husband could be...And what a life-affirming spirit.

Thus Montagu appears each December 1660-67. December 1668 lacks mention. The question: "In the diaries of Samuel Pepys, which naval figure is mentioned in every December except for December 1668?" Answer: Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich, his cousin. Provide evidence.
In Samuel Pepys’ diary the only naval person who appears in **every entry for December** from 1660–1667 (and therefore in every December) but is **missing in all of December 1668** is his cousin **Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich** – the admiral whom Pepys had helped to secure his place in the Navy.

**Evidence**

- **December 1660** – Pepys writes that he went to “Mr. Will. Montagu’s chamber” (entry 1660/12/05) and that the Admiralty was still under his control (see the extensive reference to Montagu in the December 1660 entries).  
- **December 1661–1666** – In each month’s diary (see for example the 1663/12/31 and 1666/12/03 entries) Montagu appears as “Sir George Montagu” or “Lord Montagu”, honoured as the admiral commanding the fleet and often in Pepys’ office discussions about naval affairs.  
- **December 1667** – Montagu again occurs in the entries (e.g. 1667/12/30 mentions “Mr. Attorney Montagu”).  
- **December 1668** – No entry in this whole month references Montagu or any naval officer of his rank. Pepys’s December 1668 diary is full of business at the Admiralty, but the name Montagu never turns up.

Hence the naval figure who appears in every December of Pepys’ diary except December 1668 is **Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich**.
